title: Devilled Kidneys
subtitle: Victorian spiced lamb kidneys on toast
excerpt: Devilled kidneys were once the most fashionable dish of the Victorian breakfast table: lamb kidneys cooked fast in a spiced butter sauce of mustard, Worcestershire sauce, cayenne, and lemon, served on toast. They fall in and out of fashion but are always delicious. The technique is simple and the whole dish is ready in under 15 minutes.
sourceNotes: Devilled kidneys were one of the most popular dishes of the Victorian era, when offal was eaten at every social level. The term devilled describes the strong, spiced seasoning: mustard, cayenne, and Worcestershire sauce were the standard devil mixture used across kidneys, bones, and other meats. The dish appears in almost every 19th century British cookbook.

content.text: The kidneys must be trimmed of their core before cooking. Cut each kidney in half lengthways and use scissors to cut out the white fatty core. Overcooked kidneys turn grey and rubbery -- they should remain a little pink inside. The whole dish moves very fast: have the toast ready before you start cooking.
Mix the {{dijon-mustard}} mustard with {{worcestershire-sauce}} sauce and {{cayenne-pepper}} cayenne. Set aside.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} butter in a frying pan over high heat until foaming. Season {{lamb-kidneys}} kidneys with {{salt-table}} salt and add to the pan cut-side down. Cook for 2 minutes without moving. Turn and cook for 1 minute. The kidneys should be just cooked through with a slight blush inside.

Add the mustard-Worcestershire mixture to the pan and stir to coat the kidneys. Squeeze over {{lemon}} lemon juice. Cook for 30 seconds. Scatter {{parsley-flat}} parsley over. Serve immediately on {{bread-white}} toast.

items.symptom: The kidneys are grey and rubbery
items.cause: Overcooked -- they were in the pan for too long.
items.fix: Kidneys cook in 3 to 4 minutes total. They should still be just pink at the centre. A grey, fully cooked kidney becomes tough and grainy. Work fast over high heat.

content.text: Devilled kidneys were one of the great breakfast dishes of Victorian and Edwardian Britain. They appeared regularly at the country house breakfast table alongside kedgeree, kippers, and devilled bones. The dish fell out of fashion after the Second World War as offal became less popular, but it has been revived several times since and appears on the menu of traditional British restaurants.
